title: Raster vs Vector Images: Key Differences and When to Use Each
description: Explore the differences between raster and vector images. Learn about resolution, scalability, common formats, and when to choose each type for your projects.

sections.title: Introduction to Raster and Vector Graphics
sections.content: Digital images fall into two fundamentally different categories: raster and vector. Raster images, also called bitmap images, are composed of a fixed grid of individual pixels, each storing color information. Vector images are constructed from mathematical formulas that define geometric shapes, paths, and curves. This distinction affects everything from image quality and scalability to file size and editing capabilities. Understanding the difference between raster and vector graphics is essential for anyone working with digital images, whether you are a web designer, graphic artist, photographer, or business professional creating marketing materials. Each type has distinct strengths and weaknesses that make it suitable for specific applications, and many professional workflows involve converting between raster and vector formats to leverage the benefits of both.

sections.title: What Are Raster Images?
sections.content: Raster images store visual information as a grid of individual pixels, each assigned a specific color value. The image's resolution is determined by the total number of pixels, typically measured in width by height (such as 1920 x 1080) or as total megapixels. Common raster formats include JPG for photographs, PNG for web graphics with transparency, GIF for simple animations, BMP for uncompressed images, and TIFF for professional photography and printing. Raster images excel at representing complex scenes with subtle color variations, gradients, and fine textures—qualities that make them ideal for photographs, digital paintings, and scanned documents. However, they have a fixed resolution: enlarging a raster image beyond its original dimensions requires interpolating new pixels, which results in visible blurriness or pixelation. Each raster format also applies different compression methods, affecting the balance between file size and image quality.

sections.title: What Are Vector Images?
sections.content: Vector images describe visual elements using mathematical equations that define points, lines, curves, and shapes. Instead of storing color information for every pixel, a vector file contains instructions for how to draw each element: a circle might be defined by its center point, radius, line thickness, and fill color. This approach makes vector graphics infinitely scalable—you can enlarge a vector logo to billboard size without losing any sharpness or quality. Common vector formats include SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics) for web use, AI (Adobe Illustrator) for professional design, EPS for print publishing, and CDR for CorelDRAW workflows. Vector images are ideal for logos, icons, illustrations, typography, and any graphics where clean lines and precise shapes are important. Their file sizes tend to be much smaller than equivalent raster images for simple graphics, but vector formats are not well-suited for representing photorealistic scenes with complex color transitions.

sections.title: Key Differences Between Raster and Vector Images
sections.content: The most significant difference is scalability. Vector images scale infinitely without quality loss because they are resolution-independent mathematical descriptions. Raster images are resolution-dependent and degrade when scaled beyond their original pixel dimensions. Raster images excel at representing continuous-tone photographs with millions of colors and smooth gradients, while vector images are better for artwork with distinct shapes, solid colors, and precise lines. File sizes also differ significantly: a complex photograph as a raster file may be several megabytes, while the same scene represented as a vector would be impractically large if even possible. Conversely, a simple logo may be 50 KB as an SVG but 500 KB as a PNG. Raster images are edited by modifying individual pixels, while vector images are edited by adjusting the underlying paths and control points, allowing for more precise and flexible manipulation of shapes.

sections.title: Converting Between Raster and Vector
sections.content: Converting between raster and vector formats is a common need in design workflows. Converting raster to vector, known as vectorization or tracing, uses specialized algorithms to detect edges, shapes, and color regions in a pixel image and recreate them as vector paths. This works well for logos, diagrams, and simple graphics but cannot faithfully reproduce photographs. Converting vector to raster, called rasterization, is straightforward: the vector image is rendered at a specific resolution, producing a pixel grid. This is necessary for web display of SVG files on older browsers, for using vector illustrations in raster-only software, or for printing workflows that require specific resolutions. Online converters make it easy to perform both types of conversion, with settings to control output quality, resolution, and color depth.

faq.question: What is the main difference between raster and vector images?
faq.answer: Raster images are made of pixels and have a fixed resolution, making them ideal for photographs but prone to pixelation when enlarged. Vector images are made of mathematical paths that scale infinitely without quality loss, making them perfect for logos, icons, and illustrations.

faq.question: Can you convert a raster image to vector?
faq.answer: Yes, you can convert raster images to vector using a process called vectorization or auto-tracing. The results are best for images with distinct shapes, solid colors, and clear edges, such as logos and diagrams. Photographs with complex gradients and textures generally do not vectorize well.

faq.question: What file formats are raster vs vector?
faq.answer: Raster formats include JPG, PNG, GIF, BMP, TIFF, and WebP. Vector formats include SVG, AI, EPS, and CDR. Some formats like PDF can contain both raster and vector elements.

faq.question: When should I use SVG instead of PNG?
faq.answer: Use SVG for logos, icons, illustrations, charts, and any graphics where scalability and small file sizes are important. Use PNG for photographs, images with complex gradients, and any content that cannot be easily represented as vector paths.

faq.question: Are JPG files raster or vector?
faq.answer: JPG files are raster images. They store photographs and complex images as a grid of pixels using lossy compression. JPG files are resolution-dependent and will show pixelation if enlarged beyond their original dimensions.
